plan.title: AP Chemistry: Particles, Reactions & Equilibrium
plan.hook: Connect particle bookkeeping to reaction yield and equilibrium. This focused AP-level sampler is not a complete AP course or an official College Board resource.
objectives: Explain ionic charge using proton and electron counts.
Identify a limiting reactant using a balanced equation.
Compare a reaction quotient with an equilibrium constant.

sections.heading: Charge counts particles, not atom size
sections.body:
The number of protons identifies an element. A neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons. Losing electrons creates a positive ion; gaining electrons creates a negative ion. Ordinary chemical ion formation changes electron count, not nuclear proton count.

For example, an ion with 12 protons and 10 electrons has net charge +2 because the twelve positive charges exceed the ten negative charges by two. It remains magnesium because its proton count is still 12. Isotopes of an element instead differ in neutron number.

A chemical formula expresses composition. Magnesium chloride is MgCl₂ because one Mg²⁺ balances two Cl⁻ ions. The subscript belongs to the compound's composition; it is not a coefficient that may be adjusted freely while balancing a reaction. Ionic solids form extended structures, so a formula unit need not represent a separate little molecule.
sections.visual: Twelve positive proton charges and ten negative electron charges leave a net charge of +2. Changing electrons changes the ion charge; changing protons changes the element.

questions.q: Does losing two electrons change magnesium into another element?
questions.hint: Which particle count defines the element?
questions.answer: No. Element identity depends on proton count. Losing two electrons makes Mg²⁺ while leaving the nucleus unchanged.

sections.heading: A balanced equation is a ratio
sections.body:
In 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, the coefficients express particle or mole ratios: two moles of hydrogen react with one mole of oxygen to make two moles of water. They are not mass ratios, because different substances have different molar masses.

Suppose 4 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂ react completely according to this equation. The oxygen can consume only 2 mol H₂, producing 2 mol H₂O and leaving 2 mol H₂. Oxygen is the limiting reactant: it sets the theoretical maximum product. The substance with fewer moles is not automatically limiting; compare amounts against the coefficients.

Convert any supplied masses to moles before applying the ratio, then convert the product amount back if needed. If an experiment collects 8 g of product when the theoretical yield is 10 g, the percent yield is (8/10) × 100 = 80%. Yield compares actual and theoretical amounts of the same product.
sections.visual: The balanced reaction needs two H₂ molecules for each O₂ molecule. Eight H₂ and three O₂ allow three batches: six H₂O molecules form and two H₂ molecules remain.

questions.q: Why can the reactant with more moles still be limiting?
questions.hint: Compare available amounts with required coefficients.
questions.answer: A reaction may require several moles of that reactant per mole of another. Limitation depends on the ratio, not raw mole counts.

sections.heading: Equal rates do not mean equal amounts
sections.body:
A reversible reaction at equilibrium has equal forward and reverse rates. Both reactions continue, while macroscopic concentrations stay constant in an undisturbed system. The concentrations need not be equal to one another.

For the simplified reaction X ⇌ Y, define the concentration ratio Qc = [Y]/[X] at the current moment. Square brackets denote molar concentration. At equilibrium and a specified temperature, the corresponding ratio is Kc. A rigorous equilibrium constant uses activities; this concentration model is a useful introductory approximation.

If Kc = 2 but the current ratio is 0.5, Qc < Kc and net forward reaction tends to increase the ratio toward equilibrium. If Qc > Kc, net reverse reaction tends to lower it. A catalyst accelerates the approach in both directions without changing K at fixed temperature. Changing temperature can change K, so comparisons must refer to the same temperature.
sections.visual: Reactants become products while products become reactants at the same rate. The amounts remain constant, but the two sides need not contain equal amounts.

questions.q: If Qc is below Kc for X ⇌ Y, which net direction is favoured?
questions.hint: The ratio [Y]/[X] must rise toward Kc.
questions.answer: Net forward reaction tends to form more Y and consume X until the ratio reaches its equilibrium value.

questions.q: An ion has 12 protons and 10 electrons. What is its charge?
questions.explain: The net charge is 12 − 10 = +2 in units of elementary charge. Electrons have negative charge.

questions.q: Why is magnesium chloride written MgCl₂?
choices: One Mg²⁺ requires two Cl⁻ ions for charge balance
Every atom must have two protons
The equation needs any convenient subscript
It contains two magnesium atoms per chlorine atom
questions.explain: One +2 ion and two −1 ions sum to zero charge. Changing the subscript changes composition, not merely reaction amount.

questions.q: With 4 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂, what is the maximum water yield under the stated reaction?
questions.explain: One mole of oxygen supports one stoichiometric batch and gives 2 mol water. Hydrogen is in excess.

questions.q: Actual yield is 8 g and theoretical yield is 10 g. What is percent yield?
questions.explain: Use actual/theoretical × 100: 8/10 × 100 = 80%. Reversing the ratio would give 125%.

questions.q: For X ⇌ Y, Kc = 2 and Qc = 0.5 at the same temperature. What is the net tendency?
questions.explain: Qc < Kc, so the current mixture has a smaller product/reactant ratio than at equilibrium. Net forward reaction increases it.

questions.q: At fixed temperature, what does adding a catalyst change?
questions.explain: A catalyst speeds the approach to equilibrium without changing its position or equilibrium constant at that temperature.

turns.line: A balanced equation is a ratio. The limiting reactant runs out first relative to the balanced reaction ratio. Percent yield is actual product divided by theoretical product, multiplied by 100%.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Why can the reactant with more moles still be limiting?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: A reaction may require several moles of that reactant per mole of another. Limitation depends on the ratio, not raw mole counts.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: With 4 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂, what is the maximum water yield under the stated reaction?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: 2 mol. One mole of oxygen supports one stoichiometric batch and gives 2 mol water. Hydrogen is in excess.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Equal rates do not mean equal amounts. Equal forward and reverse rates can maintain unequal, constant concentrations. Comparing Q with K at the same temperature predicts the direction of net reaction.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: If Qc is below Kc for X ⇌ Y, which net direction is favoured?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Net forward reaction tends to form more Y and consume X until the ratio reaches its equilibrium value.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: For X ⇌ Y, Kc = 2 and Qc = 0.5 at the same temperature. What is the net tendency?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Forward reaction. Qc < Kc, so the current mixture has a smaller product/reactant ratio than at equilibrium. Net forward reaction increases it.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: To review: Explain ionic charge using proton and electron counts. Identify a limiting reactant using a balanced equation. Compare a reaction quotient with an equilibrium constant.
